summary:
NASA’s SPHEREx mission maps the entire sky every six months in 102 near-infrared bands, producing images of over a billion objects. No single person can evaluate this much data, and existing sky maps are flat: the depth of objects in space is not shown.

Planet X and SPHEREx lets users move through space in three dimensions, much as Google Earth Pro lets them move over the Earth. A search panel on the left finds planets, star systems and nebulae by name, and the scene moves toward the selected object. The platform uses SPHEREx’s public data from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). Planned features include a time-series player for spotting moving or variable objects, a selectable field of view, Gaia and WISE overlays, and image metadata display.

The most ambitious component is a planned AI-assisted universe mapping module. It would learn from objects with known distances, such as stars with Gaia parallax measurements, and estimate the distances of other objects from SPHEREx’s 102-band measurements, turning flat maps into three-dimensional ones. These are estimates, so they would be shown with uncertainties and kept distinct from measurements. The module is not built yet and needs sufficient data, computing power and expert support.

We aim to open SPHEREx data to non-experts, support citizen science and help students explore the universe.
details:
NASA SPACE APPS CHALLENGE 2026

PROJECT REPORT

Planet X and SPHEREx: A Three-Dimensional Space Exploration Platform

Team: HıyarX

Website: https://spherexuzayprojesi.vercel.app/

1. Summary

This report presents Planet X and SPHEREx, a web platform developed by Team HıyarX for the SPHEREx challenge of the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Much as Google Earth Pro lets users move freely over the Earth’s surface, the platform lets users move through empty space in three dimensions: up, down, forward and backward. Through the search panel on the left side of the site, users can look up objects such as planets, star systems and nebulae; the SPHEREx data related to the selected object is then displayed in the three-dimensional scene. A later stage of the project is an AI-assisted universe mapping module that will convert SPHEREx’s flat (two-dimensional) sky maps into three-dimensional maps. This module does not exist yet; it is presented as a goal that could be developed with sufficient support.

2. Problem Statement

According to the challenge brief, since May 2025 SPHEREx has been mapping the entire sky every six months in 102 near-infrared bands, producing images of more than a billion objects. This amount of data is beyond what a single person, or software alone, can fully evaluate. Discovering moving objects by comparing images has been used throughout history: Pluto was discovered this way, and citizen science projects such as Backyard Worlds have found many brown dwarfs and comets. The task is to develop an easy-to-use web tool that allows everyone to take part in such discoveries. Existing sky maps, however, are flat; the depth relationships of objects in space are not shown directly to the user.

3. The SPHEREx Mission and Data Sources

SPHEREx is a NASA Astrophysics Medium-Class Explorer (MIDEX) mission launched in March 2025. During its planned two-year mission, it performs spectroscopy across the entire sky in the 0.75–5 micron range. The data is publicly available through the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), and calibrated spectral images are released at IRSA on a weekly basis. In place of the first release (QR1), which began in July 2025, QR2 data processed with improved calibration has been the default product since October 2025. According to IRSA’s newsletter dated 13 November 2026, SPHEREx Data Release 1 (DR1) has also been published.

For data access, IRSA offers programming interfaces compliant with IVOA standards (SIA2), the pyvo and astroquery Python packages, and the SPHEREx Data Explorer web application. The data is also accessible through the Amazon Web Services Open Data repository. The proposed platform is designed to use these publicly available interfaces as its data source.

4. Project Concept and Purpose

Existing sky viewers generally present a two-dimensional map. Our project instead aims to offer users an exploration experience rather than a control panel: the user moves around inside a three-dimensional scene, finds the planet, star system or nebula they are interested in through the search box in the left panel, and heads toward that object. The purpose is to enable everyone, regardless of level of expertise, to interact with SPHEREx data and contribute to citizen science.

5. Platform Features

•      Three-dimensional navigation: Using a mouse or touch screen, the user changes direction, zooms in and zooms out within the space scene, and changes the viewing angle by moving up and down.

•      Left search panel: Planets, star systems, nebulae and similar objects are searched by name. Astronomical databases such as SIMBAD are planned to be used for name resolution. When a result is selected, the scene moves toward that object.

•      Coordinate input: The user can go directly to any region of the sky by entering Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec) values.

•      Time-series player: Images of the selected region are ordered by observation date and displayed like a video with play, pause, forward, backward and speed controls, so that moving or brightness-varying objects can be noticed.

•      Field-of-view selection: A larger field of view makes it easier to track fast-moving objects but increases data transfer time; therefore the choice is left to the user.

•      Data from other telescopes: Data from missions such as Gaia and WISE can be overlaid as layers.

•      Metadata display: Image metadata such as contamination flags is shown to the user.

•      Query by URL: Coordinates can be added to the link as parameters. Example format: [WEBSITE ADDRESS]?ra=[RA]&dec=[DEC]. This makes it easy to embed the tool in other websites.

6. AI-Assisted Universe Mapping Module (Planned)

The most ambitious component of the project is an AI-assisted universe mapping module that will convert SPHEREx’s flat sky maps into three-dimensional maps. This module has not been developed yet; it is planned as work that can be carried out once sufficient data, computing power and expert support are available.

The proposed approach is as follows: On a flat map, only the position of objects on the sky is known, not their distance. The aim is for the model to learn from objects whose distances are known (for example, stars with parallax values measured by the Gaia mission) and then estimate the distances of other objects from SPHEREx’s light measurements in 102 bands. The estimated distances will be used to position objects in the platform’s three-dimensional scene.

These outputs are model estimates, not measurements. For this reason, the platform is planned to display the estimated distances together with their uncertainties and in a way that can be distinguished from measured values.

7. Expected Impact

The platform is expected to open SPHEREx data to non-expert users as well and to contribute to citizen scientists’ discovery of objects. In educational use, it will allow students to interact with astronomical data by navigating through space.

8. Limitations and Future Work

The AI-assisted universe mapping module does not exist yet, and its success depends on the quality of the training data and the level of support that can be obtained. Large fields of view and a large number of images increase data transfer time; caching and low-resolution previews can reduce this effect. Some of the features described in this report are planned functions and will be elaborated during the development process.
